parole.testo: From Occitan -ada, from Latin -āta. Doublet of -ée.

parole.significato: a type of traditional bull run in Provence or Occitania
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan abrivado (literally “haste, impulsiveness”), from abrivar (“to hasten”).
Borrowed from Occitan. Doublet of adroit.
Borrowed from Occitan aglandau, from agland (“acorn”), referring to its shape.
From Occitan aiguada.

parole.significato: aligot (a potato and cheese dish from Auvergne)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan alicouot. Etymology obscure; possibly from Latin aliquid. Alternative theory derives it from Old French harigoter (“to rip to shreds”), from Frankish *harjōn, from Proto-Germanic *harjōną (“to attack with an army”).

parole.significato: fruit of any tree that is described under amélanchier (serviceberry).
parole.testo: From Southeastern Occitan amelanca, rebracketing with the article from melanco, containing an Ancient Ligurian suffix attached to a word for black cognate to Ancient Greek μέλας (mélas, “black”) and Latvian melns (“black”), calling the fruits by their colour.

parole.significato: a traditional Provençal spread made from anchovy, caper, olive oil and garlic
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan anchoiada, from anchòia (“anchovy”). By surface analysis, anchois + -ade.
From Middle French araire (1443), a borrowing from Occitan araire, from Latin arātrum. Compare the inherited Old French arere, which had fallen out of use in favour of charrue.

parole.significato: arbutus berry (fruit of the strawberry tree)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan arboça, from arboç, from Latin arbuteus (“of the strawberry tree”), from arbutus (“strawberry tree”).

parole.significato: synonym of ajonc de Provence, Ulex parviflorus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan arjelàs.
Borrowed from Occitan arpioun, from arpa (“claw”).

parole.significato: ravine, stream (commonly seen in toponyms in Gascony)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan arrèc, the Gascon dialectal form of standard rèc, cognate with Catalan rec and Basque erreka. Ultimately from Proto-Celtic *ɸrik- (“furrow”).

Borrowed from Occitan artichaut, arquichaut, from Lombard articioch (cf. Italian articiocco), from Old Spanish alcarchofa, from Andalusian Arabic الْخَرْشُوف (al-ḵaršūf), from Arabic الْخُرْشُوف (al-ḵuršūf).
Borrowed from Occitan aspic (“ear (of grain), lavender”), from Latin spicum. Doublet of spic.
Borrowed from Occitan avelana.

parole.significato: pit cave, pit (natural cave with predominantly vertical shafts)
parole.testo: From Occitan avenc, from Gaulish *abonā (“river”), from Proto-Celtic *abū (“river”). Compare Breton aven, avon.
Borrowed from Occitan alhòli, contraction of alh (“garlic”) + òli (“oil”).
Perhaps from Occitan baderno.
From Occitan.
Borrowed from Occitan balès.

parole.significato: return of the bulls to pasture after a bull run (abrivado)
parole.testo: Occitan bandir.
From Occitan berigola, from Latin maurucula, from Maurus (literally “Moorish”).
Occitan bartavela

From Gascon Occitan basc, from Latin Vascō, Vascōnēs pl, a pre-Roman era tribe settled in the Atlantic Biscaian gulf and Pyrenean mountain region of south-western Europe, who were ancestors of the current Basque population.
Borrowed from Occitan bastida, past participle of bastir, cognate with French bâtir. Doublet of bâtie. Compare with bâtisse.
From a combination of Occitan bellasso and standard French bellâtre.
Borrowed from Occitan bernat l’ermita (literally “Bernard the hermit”), probably named after Bernard of Clairvaux.
From Occitan or Provençal bigarrada, bigarrat, related to the origin of bigarrer (“to variegate”).

parole.significato: to variegate, to produce a colourful pattern
parole.testo: From bis (“twice”) + *garrer, from Middle French garre (“of two colors”), but further origin uncertain; possibly borrowed from Occitan or Provençal, ultimately from Germanic. Ultimate source of English bigarade (“bitter orange”).

parole.significato: uniform or coat with buttons down the front
parole.testo: 1788, of obscure origin. Three hypotheses are: * French blousse (“scraps of wool”), from Occitan lano blouso (“pure or short wool”), from blous, blos (“pure, empty, bare”), from Old High German blōz (“naked, bare”) (German bloß (“bare”)) * A conflation of the aforementioned and French bliaud, bliaut

From Occitan boumbouno m [from boumbo + -ouno, ultimately from Latin bombus and -ōnem], made feminine under the influence of French bonne (unrelated), and with change of bomb- to bonb- under the influence of French bonbon (also unrelated). By surface analysis, bombe + -on. Although less common, the
Borrowed from Occitan bordiga.
In the original sense from Occitan bòria. In the sense of shelter, a repurposing, c. 1970, of the original, obsolete term.

parole.significato: a clump of trees; a grove
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan bosquet, from Frankish *busk + -et (diminutive ending). Doublet of bochet. Compare Italian boschetto.
From Occitan bolhabaissa, possibly a compound of bolhir (“to boil”) + abaissar (“to lower [temperature]”). By surface analysis, bouillir + abaisser.
Borrowed from Occitan bolegar, which inherited it from Vulgar Latin *bullicāre. Doublet of bouger.
From Occitan bordilha (“garbage”)
From Occitan branco (“straggler, sluggard”).

parole.significato: bush, outback (wild area away from urban area)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan brossa, of the same pre-Roman origin as brocciu.

parole.significato: butcher's broom (and other plants in the genus Ruscus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan brusc, from Italian brusco. Doublet of brusque.

Borrowed from Occitan (Gascon) berret (“cap”), from Medieval Latin birretum, from Late Latin birrus (“large hooded cloak”), from Gaulish birrus (“short cloak”), from Proto-Celtic *birros (“short”) (compare Welsh byr, Middle Irish berr). Compare biretta, Catalan barret.
From Occitan cavilhòt attested in Languedoc and Gascon, derived from cavilha cognate with French cheville.
Borrowed from Occitan cabrit (“(goat) kid”), from Vulgar Latin capritus (“billy goat”). Doublet of chevri. Compare Spanish cabrito.
From Occitan (Béarnais) cacoulet, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: cadastre (a register showing details of land ownership and value)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan cathastre, from Italian catastro (modern catasto), from Venetan catastico, from Byzantine Greek κατάστιχον (katástikhon, “line by line”), from Ancient Greek στίχος (stíkhos, “line, row”). Cognate with Spanish catastro.

parole.significato: a type of chickpea pancake popular in Toulon
parole.testo: Clipped from Occitan pascada.
Borrowed from Occitan capdet, from Late Latin capitellum (“small head”). Doublet of chapiteau, cadeau, and caudillo.
From Occitan cagnoto, canhòta, cagn, cagno, cagni, from Vulgar Latin *cania, from Latin canis.
From Occitan cagòla, feminine of cacou.

From Béarnais Occitan cagot, of uncertain origin. Many hypotheses have been advanced over time, often postulating some connection with the Visigoths, in accordance with folklore and historical speculation of their mysterious origin. The predominant hypothesis today posits that it is equivalent to Oc
Borrowed from Occitan cagar, from Latin cacāre, whence also the inherited doublet chier.
Inherited from Middle French caisse, borrowed from Occitan caissa, from Latin capsa. Compare the etymological doublets châsse and casse.

parole.significato: creek (rocky inlet), especially one in the Mediterranean
parole.testo: From Occitan calanca.
Borrowed from Occitan calissoun.
Borrowed from Occitan cap, from Latin caput. Doublet of chef.
Borrowed from Occitan carnacier or Provençal carnaza, from Vulgar Latin *carnacea, from Latin carnem (“meat”).
From Occitan carrar, from Latin quadrāre.
From Occitan cacìo, from acacia. Doublet of acacia.
Borrowed from Occitan caçolet.
Borrowed from Occitan castanhòla, diminutive of castanha (“chestnut”).
Borrowed from Occitan cavala or Italian cavalla, from Latin caballa.
Borrowed from Occitan [Term?].

Attested since at least 1838, originally to denote the incomprehensible talk of Auvergnats. The further etymology is uncertain. It's believed to possibly mimick a perceived Auvergnat pronunciation of /s/ as /ʃ/. Others theorize it's derived from Occitan charrar (“to chatter”), or Franco-Provençal ch
Probably from Occitan charrada, from charrar (“to chat”). Compare Italian ciarlare.
Borrowed from Occitan cap-virar, capvirar (cf. cap and virer).
Middle French chicquenode, from Occitan chicanaudo.

Inherited from Middle French ciboule, from Old French cibole, borrowed from Occitan cibola, itself from Late Latin cēpulla~caepulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa~caepa (“onion”), whence the inherited French cive (“chive”).
Borrowed from Occitan cigonha, from Latin cicōnia. Replaced Old French çoigne, ceoigne.

Likely from clore (“to close”) + porte (“door”), from its habit of rolling into a ball. Another possible derivation is from an unattested *croteporque, mirrored in Occitan porquet de crota (“woodlouse”, literally “cave-pig”). In any case, the analysis in the first proposal is probably responsible fo
From Occitan coucoun (“cocoon”), derived from coco (“shell”).

parole.significato: large, big, out of the common
parole.testo: Clipping of Occitan comaco, from coma aquò (“like that”).
Borrowed from Occitan comtat. Doublet of comté.
Borrowed from Occitan cramar, cremar, from Latin cremō. Doublet of crémer.

parole.significato: A participant in a series of jacqueries or peasants' revolts in the South of France during the late 16th and early 17th…
parole.testo: From Occitan croucant. Further etymology disputed.
From Occitan crostada or Italian crostata. Compare Catalan crostada.
A shortened form of cèpe de Bordeaux; from the Gascon (dialect of Occitan) cep (literally “trunk”), in reference to the mushroom's fat stalk, from Latin cippus. Doublet of cep, cippe, and sep.

parole.significato: a type of mythological creature associated with the dangers of water
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan drac, from Latin dracō. Compare the doublet dragon.
Borrowed from Occitan degun, from Latin nec ūnus (“not even one”). Compare Catalan degú, Spanish ninguno, Portuguese nenhum.

Inherited from Middle French dialectal déraper (“to tear at”), from Occitan derapar, derrabar (“to tear, uproot”), from de- + rapar (“to seize, remove”), from Gothic *𐍂𐌰𐍀𐍉𐌽 (*rapōn, “to snatch, steal”), from Proto-Germanic *hrapōną, *hrēpōną (“to scratch, touch, pluck out, snatch”), from Proto-Indo-
From Occitan embardar.
From Occitan embrum, from embruma (“to drizzle”).
Borrowed from Occitan emparar, from Vulgar Latin *imparāre (the native form would be *emperer). Compare Italian imparare (“to learn”).
Calque of Occitan empegar, from pega (“glue”)
Borrowed from Occitan ensucar (“to stun”).
From Middle French ers (16th c.), from Occitan èrs, from Latin ervum (“vetch”).
From Occitan escargol, alteration of caragol, metathesis of cagaròl, see there for more. Doublet of cagouille.
Borrowed from Occitan espardilha via metathesis, itself from espart (“esparto grass”). Compare Catalan espardenya.
From Occitan esquichar.

parole.significato: to damage, ruin, or wear out, especially through use or misuse
parole.testo: From Occitan esquintar, from Old Occitan esquintar, probably from Vulgar Latin *exquintare (“divide into five”), from Latin ex- + quintus.
Borrowed from Occitan estraçar (“to tear”).
Borrowed from Occitan patin-cofin.

parole.significato: synonym of micocoulier de Provence (“European nettle tree”) (Celtis australis)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan.

parole.significato: synonym of micocoulier de Provence (“European nettle tree”) (Celtis australis)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan.
Borrowed from Occitan fadatz.
Borrowed from Occitan fadeza, fadeso (“foolishness, self-satisfaction, complacency”), ultimately from Latin fatuus. Compare fade (“insipid”).
Borrowed from Occitan fadar.

parole.significato: a stratum chiefly composed of shell beds, usually in reference to certain marine Cenozoic deposits in France
parole.testo: Likely from Occitan falun.
Borrowed from Occitan farandola.

From Occitan farfadet, from fadet, by addition of the expressive affix particle far- → see farfouiller,[1] with influence from Italian farfarello or Arabic فرفار, farfar ("inconsistent, fickle"), from farfara ("to agitate, stir")[2][3].
From Middle French flammant (16th c.), from Occitan flamenc.

parole.significato: a type of dessert cake similar to clafoutis
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan flaunharda, from flaunhar (“flatter, fawn, spoil”).

parole.significato: a type of creamy blue cheese made from cow's milk
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan forma, from Latin fōrma. (Cf. fromage “cheese”.) Attested since the early 19th century. Doublet of forme.
From Occitan felibre.
Borrowed from Occitan gabarra.
From Occitan gagas, from Latin gagates

Borrowed from Occitan galejada.
Borrowed from Occitan gamacha, from Spanish guademecí, from Arabic غَدَامِسِيّ (ḡadāmisiyy, “related to the town of غَدَامِس (ḡadāmis) in Tripolitania”).
Probably from Occitan ganso, from Ancient Greek γαμψός (gampsós, “curved”).
Borrowed from Occitan garbura.

parole.significato: An Occitan cowboy in the Camargue region
parole.testo: From Occitan. Doublet of gardien.
Borrowed from Occitan garopa, also Medieval Latin garropa in the 11ᵗʰ century, ultimately a substrate.
Borrowed from Occitan garriga, perhaps from a pre-Roman *carra (“stone”).
Borrowed from Occitan nhac (“biting”).
From earlier agriotte, borrowing of Occitan agriota, a derivative of agre (“sour”). Compare Italian agriotta (“sour cherry tree”).

From Occitan gus.

parole.significato: hatchet, small axe (as traditionally used in Landes of Gascony)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan hapchòt.
Borrowed from Occitan hardes (Gascon and Béarnese), corresponding to standard Old French farde, from Arabic فَرْدَة (farda, “single piece”).
Borrowed from Occitan isard, possibly from a Pre-Roman (Basque or Iberian) root *izarr-, *isarr-.
From Occitan jatz, from Vulgar Latin *jacium, from jacēre, jaceō. Compare gésir (“to lie, to be buried”) and gîte (“lodging”).
Borrowed from Occitan qu'es aquò? (“what is it?”).

parole.significato: Occitan (an endangered Romance language spoken in Occitania, a region of Europe that includes Southern France, Auvergne…
parole.testo: Literally, “language of oc”, from Occitan òc (“yes”). Compare langue d'oïl and langue de si.
Derived from Occitan lecha.
Borrowed from Occitan lusèrna (“glowworm”), a reference to its shiny seeds, from Latin lucerna (“lamp”).
From Occitan manada, from man (“hand”).

parole.significato: farm, ranch, (country) house (type of rural farmstead in Occitan-speaking territories)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan mas, from Latin mānsum.
Borrowed from Occitan mascaret (“steer with a mottled face”). The appearance of the tidal bore was thought to resemble a herd of stampeding cattle.
Borrowed from Occitan mesclum (“mixture”), from Early Medieval Latin misculāre.

parole.significato: Fruit of the hackberry (tree of the genus Celtis)
parole.testo: From micocoulier or borrowed from Occitan micocola.
From Middle French micocoulier, itself from Occitan micocolièr. Ultimately from Greek.
Unknown. Possibly from a metathesis of Occitan vorm, vorma (cf. also Catalan borm), akin to French gourme, itself from Frankish *wurm; cf. English worm. Alternatively, derived from Latin morbus.

parole.significato: a stack shaped like a haystack
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan molon. related to meulon (“haystack”).
Borrowed from Occitan muge, from Vulgar Latin *mūgō (cf. Italian muggine), a noun based on Latin mūgil (“mullet”).
Borrowed from Occitan. By surface analysis, Nice + -ard.

parole.significato: nougat (sweet confection with egg white and almonds or nuts)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan nogat, from noga (“nut”).
Borrowed from Occitan ola (“marmite”).

parole.significato: a pocket shaped fishing net for catching small fish
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan pacholo. Sense 3 is likely under influence from cagole.
From Occitan palomba, from Latin palumba.
Borrowed from Occitan panicaut, from Vulgar Latin *panecaldus, alteration of Gaulish Latin *panecardus, from panis + cardus.
Borrowed from Occitan parpalhòt (“butterfly”), probably an allusion to the infidelity of Protestants who "flutter from church to church".
Borrowed from Occitan pastis or Old Occitan pastis, pastitz, from Vulgar Latin *pastīcius, from Late Latin pasta. Doublet of pastiche, which was taken from Italian pasticcio. Compare also pâtisser.

parole.significato: Used to express compassion, surprise or pity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan pechaire (the Vivaro-Alpine form of pecaire, used in Provençal too as an interjection), from Latin peccātor (“sinner”). Doublet of pécaïre.

parole.significato: a Provençal olive cultivar originally from Gard
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan picholina.
Borrowed from Occitan pichon (“small, little”).
Borrowed from Occitan pinha, from Latin pīnea.
Borrowed from Occitan pineda, from Latin pīnēta.

parole.significato: pistou (cold sauce made from cloves of garlic, fresh basil, and olive oil)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan pistou, from Late Latin pistāre (“to crush”).
Borrowed from Occitan ponen, ponent, from Latin pōnēns, present participle of pōnō (“to set”), in reference to the setting sun. Doublet of pondant.

parole.significato: A steep and narrow stairway in the medieval town
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan ; ultimately from Latin posterula.
Borrowed from Occitan poton.

Borrowed from Occitan preire (“priest”), ultimately from Latin presbyter. Doublet of prêtre.
From Occitan pebrino, from Occitan pebre, from the resemblance of the brown dots on the silkworm to pepper.
Borrowed from Occitan pecaire.
Borrowed from Occitan pegar.

parole.significato: rest, remainder, leftovers, extra food; (especially) in a canteen, where using which, one can ask for some extra food f…
parole.testo: Clipping of rabiot (“(originally fishermen and military cant) excess, remainder; (earlier) (1831) excess of fish remaining after rations had been imparted to the mates, (1859) soup soldiers often left over in their mess tin, (1832) an extra something which one can enjoy”). Further unclear, probably
Borrowed from Occitan rasclar, from Vulgar Latin *rasclare, from Latin rasculum, from rasus (“razor”). Doublet of râler. Compare also Italian raschiare.
Borrowed from Occitan rascassa.

parole.significato: a traditional French Provençal stewed vegetable dish consisting primarily of tomatoes, zucchini and eggplant, with othe…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan ratatolha (ratatouille is a dish from Nice, in Provence), French form from diminutive prefix tat- + touiller (“to stir”), from Latin tudiculō (“to grind, mix”).

Analysable as rebrousser + -ier, but said to be from Occitan rebroussiè (“churlish, surly; the opposite to others”), from Latin reburrus (“with bristling hair”). Compare à rebours and à rebrousse-poil, both ultimately from the same Latin word.
Borrowed from Occitan resquilha, from esquilha.

parole.significato: A type of dry stone wall supporting a terrace in Provence, or the terrace itself
parole.testo: From Occitan restanca.
Borrowed from Occitan robinhòla.
Borrowed from Occitan rosta (“thrashing”).
Borrowed from Occitan remolada, from re- + mòler (“to grind”).
From Occitan sanqueta, from sang (“blood”) + -eta (diminutive suffix). By surface analysis, sang (“blood”) + -ette (diminutive suffix).
From Occitan escoba (“broom”). Popularised by Alexandre “Sacha” Distel’s 1958 song “Scoubidou”.

parole.significato: maid (female servant (role) in a theatrical performance)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan soubreto.

parole.significato: to heave (pull hard on a rope, oars, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan socar, from soca (“stump, stock”).
Borrowed from Occitan tapenada.

parole.significato: of, from or relating to the city of Toulouse, the prefecture of the Haute-Garonne department and the Occitania region,…
parole.testo: From Toulouse + -ain or from Occitan tolosan/tolosenc.
Borrowed from Occitan torrer or tour + -ier.
Borrowed from Occitan ubac, from Latin opācus. Doublet of opaque.

From Middle French (plural variolez attested), borrowed from Occitan variola or directly from Medieval Latin variola, itself derived from Latin varius. Cognate to English variola, Italian vaiolo, Spanish viruela, Bulgarian вариола (variola).

parole.significato: of, from or relating to territories of the Papal States in Southern France
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan venessin, perhaps related to Venasque.
Probably from Occitan vinassa, from Latin vīnācea. First attested in the mid–18th c. By surface analysis, vin + -asse.
Borrowed from Occitan vei!, imperative of veire (“to see”).
From Occitan euse (older forms elze), derived from an Osco-Umbrian form of Latin ilex.
Borrowed from Occitan zo, onomatopoeic.

Borrowed from Spanish borrico (“donkey”) or from Occitan borrica (“jenny”), from Latin burricus (“small horse”), from burrus (“red, reddish-brown”), which is itself from Ancient Greek πυρρός (purrhós, “flame colored”), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).

Probably from a Norman or Picard word equivalent to French champ (itself inherited from Old French champ and Latin), from Old Northern French camp, from Latin campus, or alternatively from Occitan camp, Old Occitan camp, possibly Italian campo. Doublet of campus and champ.

Inherited from Middle French escallier, borrowed (through written form) from Occitan escalier, from Late Latin scālārium (attested in some inscriptions), neuter nominalization of *scālārius (“pertaining to a flight of stairs”), or from scālāris, from Latin scāla (“ladder”). parole.significato: to conjure away, to make disappear
parole.testo: Probably from an old form of Occitan escamotar, from escamar, from Latin squāma (“scale [of a fish]”). Compare Italian squamare (“to scale”). Alternatively from Spanish escamotar, from Latin excommutare.

parole.significato: synonym of thym (aromatic herb used in cooking)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan ferigoulo, farigoulo, from Old Occitan farigola, from Vulgar Latin *fericula < ferus. OR from Medieval Latin *ferricula < fer, influenced by auricula, lenticula, sanicula as well as ferraria.

parole.significato: a punch, a jab, especially one that is quick and hard to dodge
parole.testo: Of obscure origin: perhaps from Italian mandala (“send it”); from Occitan mandalo (“almond”); or from mandoline or mandarine.
